name: Neo-fascism
summary: Neo-fascism is the family of radical right tendencies and groups that took up fascism after the Second World War. Its defining sources describe it as militantly nationalist, preferring authoritarian to democratic government and totally rejecting Marxist socialism and its egalitarian ethos, while also attacking liberal market capitalism and seeking a third way. From the 1950s it reached beyond the single nation towards a united Europe opposed to both the United States and the Soviet Union, with corporatist economic ideas and a spiritual, socially conservative view of life.
scope: Post-1945 neo-fascism as the reference works and scholarship define it: political tendencies and groups after the Second World War inspired by fascism (Treccani; Encyclopaedia Judaica), above all in Italy (the MSI and the groups around it such as Ordine Nuovo) and the transnational European neo-fascist right of the 1950s (Calvert; Castelli Gattinara et al.). Answers come only from what these defining sources state about neo-fascism and its tradition, never from a single party's or group's programme (MSI, CasaPound, Forza Nuova are other subjects) nor from interwar fascism; the Encyclopaedia Judaica keeps movements aiming at a Nazi-type racial dictatorship apart as neo-Nazism.

sources.title: Neo-Fascism

sources.usedFor: Definition and shared traits: militant nationalism, authoritarian rather than democratic government, rejection of Marxist and egalitarian doctrine, xenophobia.

sources.title: Neofascismo
sources.author: Dizionario di Storia, Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana (Treccani), 2010
sources.usedFor: Definition and scope: postwar tendencies and groups inspired by fascism, the MSI and the groups around it.

abortion-legal.rationale: Marchi traces the conservative stand on abortion kept by the post-fascist right to the neo-fascist tradition's social conservatism and its Catholic, spiritual view of life.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Marchi describes the neo-fascist MSI as excluded from the 'constitutional arc' because it opposed the antifascist constitution's values; only its post-fascist successor first conceded antifascism a historical role.

assisted-dying.rationale: Marchi lists euthanasia among the bioethical questions on which the conservative values inherited from the neo-fascist tradition prevailed.

civilizational-union.rationale: From the early 1950s neo-fascists proposed a European nation-state built on shared traditions and homogeneous cultures, and the 1951 Malmö meeting launched a pan-European movement.

class-collaboration.rationale: The corporative system neo-fascists propose (Meriggi) organises employers and workers together instead of in class struggle, which neo-fascism rejects with Marxism (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

class-struggle-history.rationale: The Encyclopaedia Judaica describes neo-fascism as totally rejecting socialist and especially Marxist dogma, whose core is that class conflict drives history.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The young neo-fascists of Rauti's current took up the massification and alienation caused by liberal-capitalist consumerism (Marchi), and the Evolian youth saw materialism and runaway capitalism as the evils to check (Calvert).

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Meriggi finds that neo-fascists keep proposing a new economic system on a corporative and social base, and Castelli Gattinara et al. note the lasting myth of the Social Republic's corporatism among Italian activists.

decide-locally.rationale: Marchi describes the MSI's neo-fascism as holding a centralist conception of the state, which its post-fascist successor abandoned when it accepted federalism.

defeat-communism.rationale: Castelli Gattinara and colleagues describe Cold War neo-fascism as building its identity on communism as the enemy, and Calvert (after Griffin) calls postwar neo-fascism anti-Communist.

democracy-best.rationale: The Encyclopaedia Judaica names a belief in authoritarian rather than democratic government among the traits shared by every movement called neo-fascist.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: A proletarian dictatorship is Marxist doctrine, which the Encyclopaedia Judaica says neo-fascist movements reject totally.

direct-action.rationale: The strands split: the neo-fascist MSI always preferred the institutional, electoral route (Marchi), while the young Evolian neo-fascists condemned contesting elections as a betrayal of fascism's extra-parliamentary orientation (Calvert).

equal-outcomes.rationale: Neo-fascism rejects the universalist and egalitarian ethos underlying socialist doctrine, according to the Encyclopaedia Judaica's definition.

experts-over-public.rationale: Opposition to technocracy is one of the claims the study of CasaPound traces back to earlier neo-fascist experience.

free-trade.rationale: Neo-fascism criticises the market economy and its tradition carries the claim of a self-sufficient European autarchy, both at odds with free trade.

legalize-drugs.rationale: According to Marchi, the neo-fascist tradition's social conservatism shows in opposition to liberalising drugs, which its successor party kept.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Scholarship on neo-fascism holds that its critique of neo-liberalism and of the market economy is a central feature of neo-fascist groups.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Meriggi describes Italian neo-fascism as split between the heirs of the Social Republic, who carried on the 'republican battle' begun in 1943, and nostalgic conservatives sympathetic to the monarchy.

multipolar-world.rationale: Postwar neo-fascism wanted a united Europe standing against both America and the Soviet Union, and later Italian neo-fascists campaign against American imperialism and globalisation.

nation-first.rationale: The Encyclopaedia Judaica's definition starts from extreme, militant nationalism, and Meriggi records neo-fascists setting the fatherland above the 'empty cult of the internationalist myth'.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Neo-fascism is anti-communist yet hostile to market capitalism (Castelli Gattinara et al.; Marchi on its old critique of liberal capitalism), and its 1950s pan-Europeanism opposed both the American and the Soviet systems as materialist (Calvert).

reduce-immigration.rationale: The Encyclopaedia Judaica describes neo-fascism as driven to xenophobia and hostility toward minorities, with neo-fascist prejudice in Switzerland inspiring agitation against foreign workers.

right-to-secede.rationale: Marchi writes that the post-fascist right took from the MSI's neo-fascism its devotion to the nation and used it against the Northern League's secessionist drift.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Marchi ties the neo-fascist tradition to a spiritual conception of life opposed to Marxist materialism, and Calvert describes young neo-fascists stressing spirituality against the materialism of both superpowers.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The Marxist theory of the state as a class instrument falls under the Marxist dogma that neo-fascism totally rejects (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

strong-leader.rationale: Neo-fascism prefers authoritarian to democratic government (Encyclopaedia Judaica), which favours a ruler unhampered by parliamentary bargaining.

workers-nation.rationale: Neo-fascists put the values of the fatherland against internationalism (Meriggi) and reject the universalist ethos of Marxist socialism (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

notes: Later pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-09) bringing the 2026-10-15 audit to rules 5, prompted by search traffic (closest ideology of Nick Fuentes). The first pass rested on Wikipedia (s1, s2), Eco's essay on fascism in general (s3, a broader ideology) and a CasaPound leader's interview (s4, one organisation's platform); every answer resting only on them was nulled or replaced from the defining sources, with the old version kept in reviewHistory. Neo-fascism has no canonical text and was never the official doctrine of a state, so it has no regime record; the defining sources are the reference entries and scholarship on neo-fascism as such, and party programmes (the MSI's 1946 ten points, quoted by Meriggi; CasaPound's and Forza Nuova's platforms) were read but not used as the ideology's own. Themes searched: government (democracy, elections, leadership, constitution), economy (corporatism, markets, welfare), world (Europe, the superpowers, NATO), society (religion, family, bioethics, immigration, race), means (violence, elections) and ecology. Blocked or closed: Britannica's neofascism section (403), Copsey's chapter 'Neo-Fascism: A Footnote to the Fascist Epoch?' (Springer bot check), the European Parliament's 1985 Evrigenis report on aei.pitt.edu (bot check), del Hierro and Domper's 'Fascism reimagined' PDF at Maastricht (403), Cassina Wolff's article on democracy and corporatism in Italian neo-fascist ideology (paywalled), and Cento Bull's Oxford Handbook chapter, Gregor's The Search for Neofascism and Camus and Lebourg (not open). The first pass's one missing statement (citizenship by descent, already added to the bank as diaspora-return-right) is dropped from this audit: its only evidence was the CasaPound interview, another subject's platform, which no longer opens (403) and does not discuss neo-fascism. Most statements stay null because the open scholarship defines neo-fascism by a handful of traits; the strands (MSI conservatives, Evolian traditionalists, the social left) differ on NATO, violence and elections.
